newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Spurned by France, Taiwan develops missile.
newsitem.headline: Spurned by France, Taiwan develops missile.

text.p: Taiwan has developed its own ground-to-air missile after a deal to buy shoulder-fired Mistral missiles from France collapsed, local media on Friday quoted military sources as saying.

The China Times newspaper and state television said the military's Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology had refashioned Taiwan's home-made Sky Sword I, a short-range air-to-air missile, into a ground-to-air missile.
The institute is Taiwan's main weapons research centre.
The air force will buy unspecified numbers of the modified Sky Sword I missiles, which will be tested during the military's joint-forces Han Kwang 13 drills on June 23-24, the reports said.
The defence ministry declined to comment.

Defence Minister Chiang Chung-ling said in March that a Mistral missile deal with France had aborted, but has not commented on reports that pressure on Paris by Taiwan's arch rival -- communist China -- was to blame.
Beijing was so angered by France's 1992 sale of 60 Mirage fighters to Taiwan that it ordered its Guangzhou consulate shut and began freezing French firms out of Chinese contracts.
Paris relented in 1995 with a vow to stop arming Taiwan, though France is honouring the Mirage deal.

Taiwan has fared better in the United States, managing to buy 150 F-16 jet-fighters, batteries of Gulf War-tested Patriot antimissile missiles and 1,299 Stinger shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles despite Beijing's protests.
Taiwan began developing its own advanced weapons after the United States and other supporters switched diplomatic ties two decades ago to Beijing.
Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949 and opposes any arms sales to the Nationalist-ruled island as infringing Chinese sovereignty.
Since the 1980s, Taiwan has developed anti-ship Hsiung Feng missiles, anti-aircraft Sky Bow and Sky Sword missiles and even a home-grown warplane, the Indigenous Defence Fighter.
Taipei says it must maintain a strong defence in the face of Beijing's longstanding pledge to use force against Taiwan if it abandons its pro-unification policy and opts for independence.

Beijing staged a series of war games and missile tests near Taiwan around the island's first direct presidential election in March 1996 in what it acknowledged was a bid to chill strong independence sentiment on the island.
